overview: This file concerns proposals during the Allied occupation to change Japan from left-hand to right-hand road traffic. It begins with a State Department memorandum compiling the side of the road used throughout the world, followed by an inquiry into whether General MacArthur and the U.S. Army had considered changing Japan’s system. An outgoing airgram then asks the U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo for a fuller assessment, and duplicated incoming copies explain that a 1946 Eighth Army proposal had been rejected because of conversion costs, disruption to streetcars and buses, Japanese objections, anticipated British opposition in Allied bodies, legal concerns about altering local customs under occupation, and the priority placed on economic stabilization. Despite the broader file title, the surviving documents deal almost entirely with automobile traffic rules rather than carrier pigeons or bus-line regulation generally.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on driving sides in selected countries
subfiles.about: Provides a worldwide country-by-country compilation showing whether road traffic keeps to the right or left.
subfiles.summary: Whitmack reports information compiled by Mr. Disdier from the American Automobile Association and from embassies and legations in Washington. The three-page table covers the Americas, Europe, Africa, Asia, and Oceania, identifying Japan as a left-driving country. It establishes the comparative international background for the later discussion of changing Japan’s rule of the road.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the “Rule of the Road” in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports preliminary findings on whether the U.S. Army had considered changing Japan to right-hand traffic.
subfiles.summary: Hulick replies to an earlier inquiry from Mr. Kelly and states that neither a file nor detailed information could be located at the Pentagon. General MacArthur had reportedly considered a change in 1945 but abandoned it as impractical. The decisive issue was the expense and difficulty of converting streetcars, tracks, and associated equipment designed for left-hand operation.

subfiles.title: Outgoing airgram A-8 requesting a study of changing Japan’s traffic direction
subfiles.from: Department of State; Robert A. Lovett, Acting
subfiles.about: Requests a detailed assessment of whether the occupation offers a practical opportunity to change Japan from left-hand to right-hand traffic.
subfiles.summary: The Department argues that most countries already drive on the right and that Japan’s occupation by American forces, together with the prevalence of American vehicles, might make conversion unusually feasible. It acknowledges the high cost of modifying streetcar switches, overhead wires, signs, and signals, and notes that the Army had rejected the proposal in 1945 without preserving a detailed file. The airgram asks Tokyo to report how fully the issue had been studied and whether useful action could now be initiated, especially before the anticipated August 1949 United Nations road-traffic conference.

subfiles.title: Tokyo airgram A-29 on the rejected traffic change proposal, retrieved copy
subfiles.about: Reconstructs the 1946 proposal to introduce right-hand traffic in Japan and explains why occupation authorities rejected it.
subfiles.summary: The airgram reports that the Commanding General of the Eighth Army proposed conversion in March 1946 because 80–90 percent of motor traffic consisted of American-made vehicles, and that a GHQ staff study initially recommended the change. Japanese and U.S. engineers estimated very large costs for altering streetcars, signals, switches, and thousands of buses, with work continuing for three years. The Japanese Government Liaison Office opposed conversion, while the Commander-in-Chief anticipated insurmountable British resistance in Allied bodies; other objections concerned the law of occupation and interference with local custom. GHQ therefore regarded the proposal as a dead issue, particularly under the current emphasis on economic stabilization.

subfiles.title: Record-copy replacement notice for Tokyo airgram A-29
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Communications and Records
subfiles.about: Designates an attached copy of Tokyo airgram A-29 as the record copy replacing an unreturned original action copy.
subfiles.summary: The form documents the Department’s records-management procedure after the original action copy was not returned to central files. It identifies the associated item as A-29 from Tokyo and gives the decimal file number 894.7971/2-849. The printed notation “M-184 11-9-48” appears to be a form or revision identifier rather than the date of this filing action.

subfiles.title: Tokyo airgram A-29 on the rejected traffic change proposal, received copy
subfiles.about: Provides a received duplicate of Tokyo’s detailed history and assessment of the proposed switch to right-hand traffic in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This copy, recorded as received on February 17, repeats the account of the Eighth Army’s March 1946 initiative and the favorable April 1946 GHQ staff study. It supplies estimates for modifying fixed streetcar installations and more than 3,000 buses, noting that the Army Chief Engineer reduced the projected cost from ¥100 million to ¥84 million. It records Japanese opposition, predicted British resistance in the Allied Council for Japan and Far Eastern Commission, and concerns that an occupying power could not alter a nonsecurity-related local custom. The proposal was considered definitively rejected, with economic stabilization making renewed action unlikely unless a means of financing it could be found.

interest: The file gives an unusually detailed view of how a seemingly technical traffic rule became entangled with occupation law, Allied diplomacy, Japanese administrative preferences, infrastructure scarcity, and postwar economic policy. Particularly valuable are the cost estimates, material requirements, implementation timetable, and recollection that some local military-government teams may briefly have imposed right-hand traffic before Tokyo sought a uniform ruling. The worldwide comparison and reference to the planned 1949 United Nations road-traffic convention place the Japanese debate within a broader effort to standardize international motoring. The duplicated airgrams and record-copy notice also illuminate State Department filing practices and permit comparison of slightly differing textual and numerical versions.
